analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal contracts with for-profit prison companies and improves help for people leaving prison.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2023 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the federal Bureau of Prisons and the U.S. Marshals Service from paying private, for-profit companies to run prisons and halfway houses, phasing out existing contracts over six to eight years. It would also require annual inspections of jails used by the Marshals Service, and require prisons to give people leaving custody counseling on expunging records, finding work, applying for food assistance, Medicaid, a driver's license, and registering to vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People held in federally contracted private prisons and halfway houses, and people leaving federal prison, who would get structured help with reentry. Federal employees would gain because core correctional work would have to be done by government staff. Taxpayers could benefit if public operation proves cheaper than private contracts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal prisoners and people reentering society

how_it_helps.text: All core correctional services at federal facilities would have to be performed by government employees six years after enactment, ending contracts with for-profit prison operators, with a narrow exception for state and local government facilities [S3].
Contracts with for-profit companies to run community confinement facilities such as halfway houses would be prohibited eight years after enactment [S3].

People released from federal custody would receive information and counseling on expungement, employment and education programs, and help applying for food assistance, Medicaid, Social Security, a driver's license, and voter registration [S3].
The U.S. Marshals Service would have to inspect every jail it uses each year to confirm it meets constitutional and federal standards [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit prison companies would lose federal contracts worth billions of dollars over time. The Justice Department would bear the cost of transitioning facilities to government operation, conducting inspections, research, and reporting, and running new reentry counseling programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison companies and federal agencies

drawbacks.text: The transition would require the federal government to hire or absorb staff and take over or replace privately run facilities, a costly undertaking that the bill does not fund or fully specify [S3].
The phase-out timeline is long — six years for prisons and eight years for halfway houses — so many current contracts would continue for years after enactment [S3].

Supporters of private facilities argue that contractors can add beds faster and more cheaply than the government can build capacity, and abrupt contract losses could strain state and local jails that house Marshals Service detainees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real problem — for-profit facilities holding federal prisoners have repeatedly drawn scrutiny over conditions — and pairs the phase-out with genuinely useful reentry requirements. Its weaknesses are that it sets long timelines, provides no funding for the transition, and relies entirely on agency reporting and rulemaking to work. Weighing benefits against costs, it would likely have helped confined and released people more than it cost the public, but it never advanced far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2023, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the End For-Profit Prisons Act of 2023 on January 20, 2023 [S1].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which was its only committee action [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit prison companies are better off: their federal contracts remain intact because the bill never moved, and people in private federal facilities got no new protections or reentry help.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison companies keep their contracts

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its only champion; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no Republican or other Democrat cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of potential opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Private prison operators (companies running federal prisons and halfway houses)
industries.note: The bill would phase out their federal contracts over six to eight years, transferring housing and custody of federal prisoners to government employees. Because the bill died, their federal revenue stream was left untouched [S3].

All core correctional services would have to be performed by federal employees, expanding the Bureau of Prisons workforce. Government staff would replace private contractors for the core work of confining federal prisoners [S3].
